# The Nearest Thing to an Alien

If you want to meet an alien, forget the telescopes. Go to the aquarium instead, find the octopus tank, and crouch by the glass. Quite often, it will come to you first. And staring back will be an animal that shares almost nothing with you — no ancestry within the last half-billion years, no familiar body plan, no overlap in how it senses the world — and yet there it is, inspecting you with pupils shaped like dumbbells, its skin cycling through colors like a radio scanning stations.

You and an octopus last shared a common ancestor roughly six hundred million years ago: probably a small, flattened, wormlike creature creeping over ancient seabeds, armed with a diffuse nerve net and eyespots barely capable of telling light from shadow. That little animal divided, and its descendants went separate ways. One branch led eventually to fish, to amphibians, to primates pressing keys. The other led, improbably, to the cephalopods — squid, cuttlefish, nautilus, and the boneless, soft-bodied octopus. Which means every intricate feature of an octopus brain evolved entirely independently of every intricate feature of yours. Complex nervous systems appeared on this planet at least twice. Intelligence is not a fluke confined to one lineage; it is a trick the Earth evidently knows how to perform.

And it performs it strangely. The common octopus packs roughly half a billion neurons — about a dog's worth — but nearly two-thirds of them reside not in the head at all. They're distributed down the arms. A severed octopus arm keeps reaching, grasping, recoiling from threats; each sucker carries chemosensory receptors, so the arm effectively tastes whatever it touches, largely without consulting headquarters. Biologists sometimes joke that an octopus has nine brains, and the joke gestures at something genuinely puzzling. Is it one self directing eight subordinates? A federation of minds? Does an octopus feel its arms the way you feel your fingers, or does it issue broad instructions downstream and trust the field reports later? Nobody knows, least of all, one suspects, the octopus.

The anecdotes stack up like testimonials. At an aquarium in Germany, keepers kept finding the overhead lights shorted out until hidden cameras caught the octopus deliberately scaling his tank at night and jetting water at a lamp he apparently loathed. In New Zealand, an octopus named Inky slipped through a gap in his tank lid one night, crossed the floor, and vanished down a drainpipe believed to lead to the sea — a breakout accomplished solo, with no blueprint. Decades earlier, at a seaquarium in Miami, crustaceans kept disappearing from a neighboring tank, and the mystery was solved only by surveillance: an octopus commuting across the floor under cover of darkness, raiding, returning home before dawn. Lab octopuses learn to unscrew jars for crabs inside. They recognize individual people, too — more than one facility has reported an animal making a habit of drenching a particular volunteer with precisely aimed jets of water while leaving everyone else dry.

Then there is the skin, which borders on sorcery. Millions of chromatophores sit across its surface, each an elastic sac of pigment that snaps wide or pinches shut in fractions of a second, layered above reflecting cells that shimmer blue and green. With these the octopus paints itself into the seascape — matching not just the colors of coral and sand but their textures, raising flaps and bumps across its body to impersonate a clump of weed. Here is the mystery: experiments suggest octopus eyes are poor at telling colors apart. Yet they match colors exquisitely. One seductive hypothesis holds that light-sensitive proteins occur in the skin itself, letting the animal register different wavelengths across its whole surface — to experience color, perhaps, not as sight but as geography, a map draped over its own body.

Stranger still, octopuses revise their own genetic instructions on the fly. Where most creatures treat the flow of information from DNA to RNA as scripture, these animals edit vast numbers of RNA messages before they're used — tens of thousands of revision points, possibly tuning nerve proteins to shifting temperatures. The price, some researchers speculate, is that genomes so intensively edited must stay conservative over evolutionary time: flexibility purchased with stagnation. Artistry traded for stability.

All this brilliance burns fast. Most species live a year or two; even the giant Pacific octopus rarely sees four. Mating flips a switch somewhere deep in the nervous system, and decline begins. A female stops eating. She attaches her eggs in strands, fans oxygen over them, defends them fiercely, and wastes away while she waits — a mind the equal of any dog's, spending its final weeks in deliberate starvation. Classic experiments showed that if surgeons remove the optic gland, she abandons the vigil and lingers months longer; the schedule is written into hormones, not necessity. Her last act is to die guarding embryos she will never teach a single thing.

That absence may be the deepest strangeness of all. Because octopuses die young and live solitarily — the mother gone by hatching day, the father departed long before — each generation begins from zero. Nothing crosses the gap from one life to the next. Imagine our species stripped of grandparents, teachers, books, gossip, warnings: every infant reinventing fire alone. Uncountable billions of octopuses have lived and died on this planet, each one cracking puzzles, fooling predators, memorizing faces, and taking the whole archive to the grave. Their kind produces genius the way fireworks produce light: spectacular, everywhere, cumulative never.

So stand at the glass anyway. Two branches of life, separated since animals were barely animals, have converged on the same improbable invention — awareness turned outward, attention paid. When the octopus drifts over, spreads its arms across the panel, and trains those odd horizontal pupils on you, neither party understands much about the other. But the curiosity on both sides of the glass is real, and it is related — the same rare instrument, built twice, by accident, in the dark. We spend fortunes listening for signals from distant stars. Meanwhile, in a tank three feet below eye level, something alive and clever and utterly unlike us is doing exactly the same thing: reaching out, curious, waiting to see what we are.

The user is asking me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open-ended creative writing prompt with no constraints on topic. I should choose something that genuinely interests me and write about it in an engaging way.

What could I write about? Options include:
- A personal essay about curiosity, consciousness, or something philosophical
- A meditation on language, time, or memory
- A short fiction piece
- An exploration of something scientific that fascinates me
- Something about the nature of conversation itself

Since I'm being asked to write "freely," this seems like an invitation to pick something I'd genuinely want to explore. Let me think about what would make for compelling reading at ~1000 words.

Some ideas:
1. The octopus as an alien intelligence — this is genuinely fascinating material (their distributed neurons, independent arm cognition, short lifespans despite intelligence)
2. The concept of liminal spaces
3. Time perception — why summers felt longer as children
4. The history of a single word
5. Something meta about what it's like to be what I am — though I should handle this carefully, not making it maudlin or overwrought
6. Mountains, geology, deep time
7. The invention of the color blue / how humans perceived colors historically
8. Libraries and the preservation of knowledge
9. Sleep and dreams
10. The entropy of things — decay, ruins

I think the octopus idea is strong because it combines science, philosophy, and wonder. Peter Godfrey-Smith wrote beautifully about this in "Other Minds." There's rich material: the fact that two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, the question of whether each arm has its own semi-independent experience, the evolutionary distance between us (we split from cephalopods over 500 million years ago), their strange lifespans (they die shortly after mating/reproducing, often through self-destruction), their ability to edit their own RNA.

Alternatively, deep time and geology could be wonderful — standing at the Grand Canyon, the rock layers as pages of a book...

Or I could do something more personal/reflective about consciousness and conversation.

Actually, let me consider writing about octopus intelligence because it naturally weaves together wonder, philosophy of mind, evolution, and mortality. It has natural narrative movement: start with the strangeness, move through the biology, explore the philosophical implications, end with the poignancy of their brief lives and what that says about mind and death.

Let me draft mentally:

Opening: Meeting an octopus is the closest we come to meeting an alien. Or start with a specific scene — an octopus in an aquarium recognizing a keeper, squirting water at a light to turn it off.

Middle sections:
- Evolutionary distance: our last common ancestor was a wormlike creature ~600 million years ago. It may have had simple eyespots. Everything complex about nervous systems evolved twice.
- Distributed cognition: 500 million neurons (comparable to a dog), but two-thirds in the arms. Arms can solve problems when severed from central brain. What is it like to be a thing whose thinking is spread across eight semi-autonomous limbs?
- Their intelligence in action: opening jars, escaping enclosures, remembering individuals (研究人员 they sprayed with water), carrying coconut shells for shelter (tool use), camouflage so sophisticated it's thought to be partly "seeing with their skin" — opsins in their skin responding to light.
- RNA editing: they edit their own RNA extensively, possibly to adapt to temperature changes — flexibility purchased at the cost of slow genetic evolution.
- The tragedy: most live only 1-2 years. The famous example — Godfrey-Smith's observation of a dying octopus, listless, colors fading. Octopuses starve themselves after mating; the optic gland secretes hormones that doom them. A mother guards her eggs, not eating, dying as they hatch.
- Why don't they develop culture? Because knowledge dies with each generation — no childhood with mothers teaching, no transmission. Each generation starts fresh. Intelligence without accumulation.
- Closing reflection: what this tells us about minds — that intelligence can bloom elsewhere, differently, ephemerally. When you look at an octopus, it looks back. Two experiments in awareness, separated by half a billion years, briefly overlapping.

That's a solid structure for ~1000 words. Let me think about tone: wonder-filled but precise, avoiding purple prose excess, using concrete details. First person observations are fine ("the closest thing we have") but shouldn't overdo claims.

Facts to verify from memory:
- Octopus vulgaris has around 500 million neurons. Yes, roughly.
- Two-thirds of neurons are in arms: yes, commonly cited figure (~350 million in arms).
- Last common ancestor with humans: cephalopods diverged from the lineage leading to vertebrates roughly 550-600 million years ago — commonly cited as around 600 million, or "more than half a billion years."
- Common ancestor likely a flatworm-like creature: Godfrey-Smith describes it as a small flattened worm-like animal with primitive eyespots. Good.
- Octopus escaping from tank: Inky the octopus in New Zealand escaped through a drainpipe to the sea (2016). The lamp-short-circuiting story: staff noticed lights flickering; camera showed Otto climbing up and squirting water at the lamp. Good detail.
- Octopus spraying disliked keeper: at University of Otago? Actually the story is about an aquarium where an octopus sprayed water at one particular person she didn't like. In "Other Minds," Godfrey-Smith mentions an octopus at a New Zealand university lab that squirted water at a particular researcher/visitor she disliked. I'll phrase carefully.
- Coconut shells: Veined octopus (Amphioctopus marginatus) carrying coconut shell halves — documented in 2009 paper by Finn, Tregenza, Norman — considered tool use. Good.
- Skin vision: cephalopod skin contains opsins, light-sensitive proteins; evidence suggests light detection in skin, particularly in some species. It's plausible/hypothesized that skin sensing contributes to camouflage. Phrase as "some scientists suspect" or "may."
- RNA editing: documented that coleoid cephalopods (octopus, squid, cuttlefish) heavily edit their RNA (Eisenberg & Rosenthal research, published 2015/2017). Trade-off hypothesis: heavy RNA editing slows genome evolution because editing machinery requires stable neighboring sequences. Phrasing: editing allows adaptation flexibility; possible trade-off. Should present it honestly.
- Optic gland controlling senescence: yes — classic experiments removing optic gland extended lifespan of female octopuses. The optic gland is analogous to pituitary, secretes hormones after egg-laying that trigger terminal behavior. Recent work (2018, Wang et al.) identified cholesterol-based signaling molecules. Fine to mention generally.
- Lifespan: giant Pacific octopus lives maybe 3-4 years; many species 1-2 years. So "rarely more than a few years."
- Male octopuses also undergo senescence post-mating.
- Density paradox: octopuses flourish in shallow waters where predation pressure is high; selection favored intelligence along with other defenses. Godfrey-Smith argues arms race between predators/prey requiring behavioral flexibility — mammals and cephalopods both evolved big brains partly due to interaction: "If we can trace our pedigree back... then the common ancestor might have been a simple vermiform... maybe it had simple eyes..."

Around 1000 words as requested. No title needed necessarily, but a short evocative title could be nice. Actually a title would be a nice touch for an essay. Let me go with something evocative.

Hedge: "one seductive hypothesis."

RNA para: More uncanny: they edit their own genetic instructions. Where we mostly trust DNA→RNA→protein pipeline, coleoid cephalopods recode huge numbers of RNA messages before translation — tens of thousands of sites(?). In 2015 study Eisenberg/Rosenthal: tens of thousands of editing sites. Purpose debated — possibly adapting nerve proteins to temperature. Cost: theory that heavy editing constrains genome evolution, slowing change, since the editing apparatus needs consistent templates. Trade artistry for stability. Keep concise and hedged.

Females stop eating, guard their eggs... eggs strung like clusters of teardrops/streamers, aerating them, defending them, fading... Without optic gland removal experiments: scientists found removing optic gland extended life. She starves among/of her own vigil, drifting toward death as/while the young hatch, and her last act/hours... The male drifts similarly, wandering, confused, colors dimming, prey unattended. A philosopher (Godfrey-Smith) encountering one such individual, senescent in a shelter, described it as like sitting with someone at the end. What strikes: enormous mind designed/with a clock attached/use-by date such that wisdom never accumulates.

Because they die young and solitary (no parental teaching — mother dead by the time eggs hatch, father long gone), each generation starts from zero. Nothing passes hand to arm (nice line). Our kind stores knowledge outside our bodies — books, songs, now servers — ratcheting generation by generation. Their kind invents genius anew and drops it. Somewhere out there, most likely, trillions(?) — hmm, careful: octopus populations large; "untold billions of octopuses have lived and died..." Each one solving jars, opening shells, foiling keepers — brilliant, isolated flashes... fireworks rather than sunrise.

Intelligence on Earth isn't a pyramid/heights with a peak called us; it's islands in two archipelagos...
